title: What is & How to Do Space Optimization
description: Shrink a DP table to a few variables when transitions reach back only a little

blocks.text: Once you have a correct tabulated DP, you can often make it use far less memory. Space optimization is the technique of shrinking the table when each cell depends only on a few recent cells.
This does not change the answer or the time complexity. It only reduces how much you store, sometimes from a big table down to a couple of variables.
Memory limits are real. A DP that needs an n by m table can exceed the memory limit even when its running time is fine. Cutting the space lets a correct idea actually pass.
It also makes the code faster in practice, because smaller data fits better in cache and there is less to allocate.

items: Keep the exact same answer and time complexity

blocks.text: Space optimization works only when a cell depends on a small, fixed number of recent cells. If dp[i] needs the whole history, you cannot throw the table away.

blocks.caption: When dp[i] needs only dp[i-1] and dp[i-2], you never need the older cells

blocks.text: For Fibonacci, dp[i] needs only dp[i-1] and dp[i-2]. Everything older is dead weight, so we can keep just two variables.
When only the last one or two values matter, replace the whole array with that many variables and roll them forward each step.
The table of size n just became two integers. Same answer, O(1) space.
The same idea scales to grids. If each row of a 2D table depends only on the row above it, you do not need the whole grid, just one or two rows.

blocks.caption: When a row uses only the row above, collapse the 2D grid into a single rolling array

blocks.text: Here is unique-paths on a grid, reduced from a full table to a single rolling row.

Watch the update direction:

When you reuse one array for two dimensions, the loop direction decides whether dp[j-1] means the old row or the new row. Trace it carefully or you will mix values.
Space optimization is not always possible. Know when to leave the full table alone.

items: You must reconstruct the actual solution, not just its value, so you need the whole table to backtrack.
A cell depends on many far-apart earlier cells, not just recent ones.
The problem asks you to answer queries about arbitrary subproblems later.

blocks.text: In those cases the full table is the point, and trying to shrink it would lose information you need.
Start with a correct tabulated solution, then ask a few questions.

items: Which earlier cells does each cell actually read?
If only the last one or two, replace the array with that many variables.
If only the previous row, replace the 2D table with one or two rows.
Check the update direction so old and new values do not collide.
If you need to reconstruct the answer, keep the full table instead.

blocks.text: Always optimise space last, after the logic is correct. It is a mechanical final step, not the place to start.
